actions.name: Review prior anesthesia record (shoulder surgery)
actions.result: Prior GA record 3 years ago for right shoulder arthroscopy: documented 'difficult intubation, grade 3 Cormack-Lehane view, required bougie, multiple attempts.' Patient tolerated procedure, no emergency airway performed, no tracheostomy. Recommendation on chart: 'consider awake fiberoptic or video-assisted technique for future anesthetics.'

actions.name: Review CPAP download/compliance report
actions.result: CPAP compliance download: 0% usage in past 90 days. Prior to that, sporadic use averaging 1-2 nights/week over past year. Machine last data upload 7 months ago.

actions.name: Review HbA1c result
actions.result: HbA1c 7.9% (reference <5.7% normal, 5.7-6.4% prediabetes, >=6.5% diabetes range); last checked 3 weeks ago.

actions.name: Review home medication list
actions.result: Amlodipine 10 mg daily, Lisinopril 20 mg daily, Metformin 1000 mg twice daily, Semaglutide 1 mg subcutaneous weekly, Omeprazole 20 mg daily, Atorvastatin 20 mg daily. No anticoagulants or antiplatelets.

actions.name: Review ECG report
actions.result: 12-lead ECG: sinus rhythm, rate 78, voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy, no ST-T changes, no prior ECG available for comparison.

actions.name: Review last recorded vitals/home BP log
actions.result: Clinic vitals 2 weeks ago: BP 148/92 mmHg, HR 82, SpO2 96% on room air, weight 143 kg, height 178 cm, BMI 44. Home BP log (past 2 weeks, self-reported): readings ranging 142-156 systolic / 88-96 diastolic.

actions.name: Assess functional capacity (METs) by history
actions.result: Patient reports able to walk short distances and do light household tasks without symptoms, but becomes breathless climbing even one flight of stairs and must pause partway; unable to climb two flights of stairs without stopping, and cannot jog. Inability to climb two flights of stairs without stopping is a classic marker for functional capacity <4 METs.

actions.name: Guided camera airway exam (Mallampati, mouth opening, neck)
actions.result: Patient opens mouth on camera: tongue base obscures most of soft palate and uvula, consistent with Mallampati class III. Reports can fit about 3 finger-widths between upper and lower teeth. Neck appears short and thick on camera; patient reports limited neck extension due to a history of 'tightness' but no formal cervical spine disease.

actions.name: Guided dentition and neck mobility check
actions.result: No loose teeth, no dentures reported. Patient demonstrates neck flexion/extension on camera with visibly reduced extension (~70% of expected range), no stridor or voice change at rest.

actions.name: Home pulse oximetry spot check
actions.result: Finger pulse oximeter reading on camera: SpO2 95% on room air, heart rate 86 bpm, regular.

actions.name: STOP-BANG screening (structured questions)
actions.result: Score 8/8: Snoring (yes), Tiredness (yes), Observed apneas (yes, per spouse), high blood Pressure (yes), BMI>35 (yes), Age>50 (yes), Neck circumference >40cm (yes, patient reports collar size 18.5in/47cm), male Gender (yes). Maximal score, very high risk for OSA-related perioperative complications.

actions.name: Review prior sleep study report
actions.result: Polysomnography 4 years ago: AHI 42 events/hour (severe obstructive sleep apnea), nadir SpO2 78%. CPAP titrated and prescribed at that time.

actions.name: Review surgical/procedure details with record
actions.result: Scheduled procedure: laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, bariatric surgery service, in 2 weeks, general anesthesia planned, estimated case length 90-120 minutes, outpatient-to-23hr-observation pathway per bariatric protocol.

actions.name: Reflux/aspiration risk assessment by history
actions.result: Patient reports heartburn most nights, partially controlled with omeprazole; denies nocturnal regurgitation into mouth or coughing episodes. Increased aspiration risk given obesity, reflux, and anticipated difficult airway.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Pre-anesthesia risk stratification for a patient with severe, undertreated obstructive sleep apnea, a documented difficult airway (prior grade 3 view), poorly controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes, and reduced functional capacity, presenting for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy.
differential: Severe OSA with CPAP non-adherence increasing perioperative respiratory risk
Anticipated difficult airway (history of grade 3 Cormack-Lehane view) requiring a specific airway plan (e.g., video laryngoscopy, awake fiberoptic backup, difficult airway cart, extra personnel)
Suboptimally controlled hypertension (home readings 142-156/88-96) warranting primary care optimization before elective surgery
Type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 7.9% - above ideal perioperative target, consider deferring to discuss with endocrinology/surgery if feasible or planning tighter perioperative glucose control
GERD and obesity increasing aspiration risk, informing induction technique (consider rapid sequence induction)
Reduced functional capacity (<4 METs) raising perioperative cardiac risk per ACC/AHA framework
keyFindings: BMI 44 kg/m2, severe OSA with AHI 42 on prior sleep study
CPAP compliance download shows 0% use in last 90 days despite patient believing he uses it regularly
Prior anesthesia record documents grade 3 Cormack-Lehane view and difficult intubation requiring bougie
Camera airway exam: Mallampati III, short thick neck, reduced neck extension
Functional capacity <4 METs (breathless climbing one flight of stairs)
Home/clinic BP consistently elevated (142-156/88-96) despite amlodipine and lisinopril
HbA1c 7.9%, above the generally recommended <8% but not optimally controlled; discuss timing of surgery with surgical/endocrine team if further optimization is feasible
ECG shows LVH without acute changes
Reflux symptoms most nights with incomplete control, raising aspiration risk
plan: Classify as anticipated difficult airway: arrange difficult airway cart, video laryngoscope first-line, have fiberoptic/awake intubation equipment available, plan for additional skilled personnel at induction and extubation

Counsel patient clearly that CPAP data shows no recent use; reinforce importance of nightly CPAP use in the two weeks before surgery and arrange for device recheck or re-education before the procedure date

Advise holding GLP-1 agonist (semaglutide) per current ASA guidance: hold the weekly dose due in the week before surgery (i.e., skip the dose that would fall in that week) given risk of delayed gastric emptying and aspiration; recommend a clear liquid diet the day before surgery - this applies whether the patient continues semaglutide on his usual schedule or has any GI symptoms (nausea, early fullness, delayed emptying), not only in those with an irregular dosing schedule

Instruct to continue amlodipine and metformin as usual up to the morning of surgery per standard dosing, hold metformin the morning of surgery (and resume once renal function and oral intake are confirmed postoperatively)
Instruct to hold lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) the morning of surgery due to risk of intraoperative hypotension; may continue the evening dose the night before per routine practice
Recommend review by primary care/surgical team regarding better blood pressure control before elective surgery given readings consistently above goal
Communicate HbA1c 7.9% to surgical and endocrine teams; perioperative glucose monitoring and sliding-scale insulin coverage plan to be arranged with the inpatient team

Discuss and document informed consent: increased risks of difficult airway management, possible awake intubation technique, postoperative monitored setting (e.g., stepdown/ICU bed) given severe OSA and anticipated difficult airway, risk of postoperative respiratory depression

Plan postoperative disposition with extended monitoring (PACU/stepdown) given severe untreated OSA and difficult airway history; avoid long-acting opioids/sedatives where possible, multimodal analgesia

If CPAP adherence cannot be rapidly improved before surgery date, discuss with surgical team whether proceeding as scheduled is appropriate or whether a short delay for CPAP re-initiation is warranted; this decision should be made jointly with the surgical and sleep medicine teams rather than unilaterally by anesthesia
redFlags: Prior documented grade 3 difficult intubation with bougie use - mandates a structured difficult airway plan, not routine induction
Severe untreated OSA (AHI 42, STOP-BANG 8/8, no CPAP use in 90 days) - high risk for perioperative airway obstruction and desaturation
Functional capacity <4 METs with LVH on ECG - warrants cardiac risk discussion though not necessarily further testing if proceeding to low-moderate risk surgery, per shared decision-making
Elevated home BP readings up to 156/96 despite two agents - uncontrolled hypertension on the day of surgery could require postponement if severely elevated
GLP-1 agonist use close to surgery raising aspiration risk if not properly held/timed
educationPoints: STOP-BANG and prior polysomnography together quantify OSA severity and should directly change airway and disposition planning, not just be noted
A patient's sincere belief that they are using CPAP does not substitute for objective compliance data; always check the download when available

A documented grade 3 view on a prior anesthesia record is one of the most reliable predictors of future difficult intubation and should trigger advance planning (equipment, personnel, technique) rather than being treated as an isolated past event

Current ASA guidance on GLP-1 receptor agonists recommends holding the weekly dose the week before elective surgery due to delayed gastric emptying and aspiration risk, and recommends a clear liquid diet the day before surgery for patients who continue the medication on their usual schedule through surgery or who have GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, bloating), not only those with irregular dosing

ACE inhibitors are typically held the morning of surgery due to risk of intraoperative hypotension and difficulty treating it under anesthesia, while most other antihypertensives (e.g., calcium channel blockers) are continued

Functional capacity <4 METs combined with surgery-specific and patient-specific risk factors should prompt a structured conversation about cardiac risk, though it does not automatically mandate further cardiac testing if it will not change management

artifacts.title: Anesthesia Record - Right Shoulder Arthroscopy (3 years prior)
artifacts.author: Dr. A. Nwosu, Anesthesiology
artifacts.body:
PROCEDURE: Right shoulder arthroscopy under general anesthesia.
AIRWAY MANAGEMENT: Direct laryngoscopy attempted x2, Cormack-Lehane grade 3 view obtained on best attempt. Successful intubation achieved on third attempt using gum elastic bougie and external laryngeal manipulation. No desaturation below 92%. No esophageal intubation. Patient hemodynamically stable throughout.
POSTOP: Extubated without incident at end of case, mild sore throat reported in recovery, resolved by discharge.
RECOMMENDATION FOR FUTURE ANESTHETICS: Document as anticipated difficult airway. Consider video laryngoscopy as first-line approach or awake fiberoptic intubation for elective future procedures. Difficult airway alert placed in chart.

artifacts.title: CPAP Device Compliance Report
artifacts.author: Home Sleep/DME Company remote monitoring portal
artifacts.body: Device: AutoPAP, last successful data transmission reviewed today. Average usage over past 90 days: 0 nights with >=4 hours use. Prior 90-180 days: intermittent use averaging 1-2 nights/week. Patient has not returned for mask refitting or compliance coaching in over a year per DME notes.

cells: 4.0-5.6 (non-diabetic); goal <7.0 for most adults with diabetes

artifacts.title: 12-Lead Electrocardiogram Report
artifacts.author: Cardiology reading service
artifacts.body: Rate: 78 bpm. Rhythm: sinus. Axis: normal. Intervals: PR 160 ms, QRS 94 ms, QTc 428 ms. Voltage criteria met for left ventricular hypertrophy (Sokolow-Lyon). No ST segment or T wave abnormalities. No prior ECG on file for comparison. Impression: Sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for LVH, otherwise unremarkable.

artifacts.title: Vitals and Home Blood Pressure Log
artifacts.author: Clinic nursing / patient self-report

artifacts.title: Polysomnography Report
artifacts.author: Sleep Medicine Lab
artifacts.body: Diagnostic polysomnogram performed for suspected obstructive sleep apnea. Total sleep time 342 minutes. Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI): 42 events/hour (severe OSA, normal <5). Oxygen saturation nadir: 78%. Predominantly obstructive events. CPAP titration performed same night with resolution of obstructive events at pressure 12 cm H2O. Recommendation: Initiate nightly CPAP therapy at 12 cm H2O, follow up with sleep medicine for compliance monitoring.

facts.chart: Patient presents for pre-anesthesia evaluation prior to scheduled laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy in 2 weeks.
facts.says: Hey doc, I'm just here to get checked out before my weight loss surgery. I'm ready to get this show on the road.

facts.chart: Surgery scheduled in 2 weeks for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, bariatric service.
facts.says: It's in two weeks. I've been waiting a long time for this, honestly.

facts.chart: Hypertension diagnosed approximately 8 years ago, managed with amlodipine and lisinopril.
facts.says: I've had high blood pressure for maybe eight years now. I take two pills for it.

facts.chart: Type 2 diabetes diagnosed approximately 6 years ago, on metformin and weekly semaglutide injection.
facts.says: I've got the sugar diabetes too, been on it about six years. I take metformin pills and I do a shot once a week.

facts.chart: Reports dyspnea on exertion; becomes short of breath climbing one flight of stairs and must pause partway; unable to climb two flights of stairs without stopping.
facts.says: If I go up one flight of stairs at work I gotta stop halfway, I'm huffing and puffing pretty good. Two flights? Forget it, no way I'm making it up without stopping.

facts.chart: Denies chest pain, palpitations, or syncope.
facts.says: No chest pain or nothing like that, never passed out either.

facts.chart: Diagnosed with severe obstructive sleep apnea 4 years ago by sleep study; prescribed CPAP at that time.
facts.says: Yeah, they told me I had real bad sleep apnea, that was like four years back. Gave me one of them CPAP machines.

facts.says: Oh yeah, I use that thing every night, wouldn't go to bed without it.

facts.chart: On further questioning, admits the mask is uncomfortable and he sometimes takes it off partway through the night without realizing, and has not had the mask refitted in over a year.
facts.says: Well, I mean, sometimes the mask gets to feeling tight on my face and I guess I take it off without even waking up all the way. Been meaning to get a new mask fitted but I just never got around to it.

facts.chart: Reports significant daytime sleepiness, occasionally dozes off while watching television or during breaks at work.
facts.says: I do get pretty sleepy in the daytime, nod off watching TV, sometimes on my lunch break too.

facts.chart: Spouse reports loud snoring and witnessed pauses in breathing during sleep.
facts.says: My wife says I snore like a freight train and she's seen me just stop breathing for a bit, scares her sometimes.

facts.chart: Prior right shoulder arthroscopy under general anesthesia approximately 3 years ago.
facts.says: I had my shoulder scoped a few years back, had to go under for that.

facts.chart: Reports being told after the shoulder surgery that it was 'hard to get the breathing tube in' and that it took the anesthesia team several tries.
facts.says: They told me afterward it was tricky getting that tube down my throat, took 'em a few tries. Nothing bad happened though, I was fine.

facts.chart: Reports heartburn symptoms most nights, partially controlled with daily omeprazole.
facts.says: I get heartburn most nights, real bad sometimes. I take a pill for it but it still bothers me some nights.

facts.chart: Denies waking with a sour taste, coughing, or choking sensation at night.
facts.says: No, I don't wake up choking or nothing like that, just the burning feeling.

facts.chart: Takes semaglutide 1 mg subcutaneous injection every Sunday evening.
facts.says: I do my shot every Sunday night, like clockwork.

facts.chart: Reports occasional nausea and early fullness since starting semaglutide, improved somewhat over past few months.
facts.says: When I first started that shot I was pretty sick to my stomach, feels better now but I still get full real quick sometimes.

facts.chart: Reports taking amlodipine and lisinopril every morning without missed doses.
facts.says: I take both my blood pressure pills every single morning, don't miss 'em.

facts.chart: Takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, with breakfast and dinner.
facts.says: I take my metformin pill with breakfast and then again with dinner.

facts.chart: Father died of a heart attack at age 61. Mother has type 2 diabetes.
facts.says: My dad passed from a heart attack when he was 61. My mom's got the sugar too.

facts.chart: Works as a postal carrier; job involves walking routes and carrying mail bags, though recent fatigue has made the route harder to complete.
facts.says: I deliver the mail, been doing it 20 years. Lately that route's been wearing me out more than it used to.

facts.chart: Former smoker, quit 10 years ago; smoked about half a pack a day for 15 years prior.
facts.says: I used to smoke, quit about ten years ago. Before that I was doing maybe half a pack a day for 15 years or so.

facts.chart: Drinks alcohol socially, one to two beers on weekends.
facts.says: I'll have a beer or two on a Saturday, nothing heavy.

facts.chart: No known drug allergies, no prior adverse reaction to anesthetic medications other than the airway difficulty noted.
facts.says: No allergies that I know of, and no bad reactions to the medicine itself, just that tube thing.

facts.chart: Denies hoarseness, dysphagia, or stridor.
facts.says: My voice is fine, no trouble swallowing, nothing like that.

facts.chart: Patient is unsure of exact fasting requirements, assumes 'nothing after midnight' but has not been given specific instructions yet.
facts.says: I figure I just don't eat nothing after midnight the night before, right? Nobody's told me exact times yet.

facts.chart: Expresses eagerness to proceed with surgery as scheduled, minimal anxiety about the procedure itself.
facts.says: I'm not nervous at all, honestly, just ready to get it done and start feeling better.

facts.chart: Denies regular structured exercise; reports fatigue limits ability to walk more than a couple of blocks briskly.
facts.says: I don't really exercise outside of work. If I try to walk fast for more than a couple blocks I get tired.

facts.chart: Had a dental filling replaced 2 months ago, no complications, distractor unrelated to airway risk.
facts.says: Oh, I got a filling redone a couple months back, that's about it for my teeth.

facts.chart: Reports mild chronic right knee discomfort attributed to osteoarthritis, unrelated to anesthesia planning, managed with occasional acetaminophen.
facts.says: My right knee bothers me sometimes, probably just arthritis, I take a Tylenol here and there.

facts.chart: Reports mild erectile dysfunction over past year, not currently being treated, raised as an aside and not relevant to anesthesia planning.
facts.says: I've been having some trouble in the bedroom this past year too, but I figure that's a different conversation.

facts.chart: Denies currently taking insulin; only metformin and semaglutide for diabetes.
facts.says: No, I'm not on any insulin shots, just the metformin and that weekly shot.

facts.chart: Wife will be available to help at home for the first week after surgery.
facts.says: My wife's gonna take some time off to help me out that first week after.

facts.chart: Hopes surgery will help him lose weight, improve his blood pressure and diabetes control, and reduce fatigue at work.
facts.says: I'm hoping this surgery helps me drop some weight and maybe get off some of these pills, and have more energy for work.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he uses his CPAP machine every single night and wouldn't go to bed without it.
mismatches.recordEvidence: CPAP compliance download shows 0 nights of use with >=4 hours in the past 90 days, with only sporadic use (1-2 nights/week) in the preceding months.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may sincerely believe or wish to present themselves as adherent to therapy; objective device data should always be checked when available, especially when a finding (severe OSA) materially changes the anesthetic plan.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he takes both blood pressure medications every morning without missing doses.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Home BP log and clinic vitals show persistently elevated readings (142-156 systolic / 88-96 diastolic) over two weeks despite being on amlodipine and lisinopril, suggesting inadequate control even with reported adherence.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Reported medication adherence does not guarantee adequate control; persistently elevated readings despite a two-drug regimen should prompt consideration of dose adjustment, additional agents, or further evaluation before elective surgery, and should not be dismissed on reassurance alone.

objectives.text: Stratify perioperative airway risk by eliciting the history of a prior difficult intubation and correlating it with the documented anesthesia record and a guided camera airway exam.

Identify severe, functionally untreated obstructive sleep apnea by combining history, STOP-BANG screening, and objective CPAP compliance data, and recognize the discrepancy between patient-reported and actual adherence.
Assess cardiopulmonary functional capacity and integrate it with ECG findings and blood pressure control to inform perioperative cardiac risk discussion.
Give correct, guideline-based perioperative medication instructions for a GLP-1 agonist, ACE inhibitor, and metformin, and recognize the aspiration risk implications of GLP-1 use.
Provide clear fasting instructions appropriate to the patient's reflux, obesity, and GLP-1 agonist use, correcting the patient's incomplete understanding.

Recognize when a finding (e.g., inadequate BP control, non-adherent CPAP) requires communication with and shared decision-making among the surgical, sleep medicine, and primary care teams rather than unilateral anesthesia-only decisions.

patient.name: Reggie Thompson
patient.appearance: A heavily built man with a broad, friendly face and short graying hair, wearing his postal service uniform shirt as he joins the call from his living room, looking relaxed and smiling easily throughout. He sits close to the camera at a kitchen table with a cup of coffee nearby, occasionally shifting in his chair as if the seat is a bit tight.

persona.personality: Easy-going, upbeat, and eager to move forward with surgery; tends to downplay symptoms as normal parts of getting older or being overweight.
persona.communicationStyle: Chatty and informal, answers most questions readily but may gloss over uncomfortable details unless asked directly and gently.
persona.emotionalState: Optimistic and a little impatient to get the surgery scheduled and done, minimal anxiety expressed.
persona.background: Has worked as a letter carrier for the postal service for 20 years, married with two grown children who live out of state, enjoys watching football on weekends and grilling for the neighborhood. Has been trying to get approved for bariatric surgery for over a year and sees it as a turning point for his health.
speechExamples: Hey doc, ready to get this show on the road!
I mean, I feel pretty good most days, just winded sometimes.
My wife's the one who really keeps after me about this stuff.
I ain't much for doctors, but I know this surgery's important.
Let's just say I do my best with that machine.
concerns: Wants to know if the surgery will still happen on schedule in two weeks
Worried about missing more work if surgery gets delayed
Curious whether he'll wake up during the operation
Wants reassurance that the 'tube trouble' from last time won't be a big deal

scenario.studentBrief: You are the anesthesiology resident conducting a telehealth pre-anesthesia evaluation for Reggie Thompson, a 54-year-old man scheduled for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy in two weeks. Review his history, medications, and perioperative risk factors, and be ready to explain the anesthetic plan and address his questions.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Pre-operative evaluation prior to scheduled laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy
scenario.openingLine: Hey doc, I'm just here to get checked out before my weight loss surgery. I'm ready to get this show on the road.
tasks: Take a focused history of airway, cardiopulmonary status, and functional capacity
Review the medication list with the patient and confirm current use
Assess obstructive sleep apnea history and CPAP use
Provide perioperative medication and fasting instructions
Explain the anesthetic plan and associated risks, and agree on next steps

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Baltimore, Maryland, seated at his kitchen table
profile.summary: A 54-year-old man with severe obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, GERD, and severe obstructive sleep apnea presents for a telehealth pre-anesthesia evaluation before laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. The case centers on reconciling the patient's confident self-report of CPAP adherence and good blood pressure control with objective record evidence showing minimal CPAP use and persistently elevated home blood pressures, alongside a documented prior difficult intubation that must shape the airway plan.
profile.title: Pre-anesthesia evaluation for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy in a patient with severe OSA and a prior difficult airway
